waypoints.name: SR-20 Wine Spires pullout (milepost 166)
waypoints.note: Unmarked highway pullout ~2-4 miles east of the Washington Pass hairpin turn; climbers descend to Early Winters Creek then switchback up to Burgundy Col.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the unsigned pullout near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass, at about 4,300 ft. There is no sign and no developed trailhead here, only a broad shoulder pullout, so watch your odometer. Check WSDOT before travelling: the highway is gated shut through the winter and reopens somewhere between mid-April and late June depending on snowpack and slide repair.

waypoints.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col
waypoints.directions: From the pullout, drop off the highway on a steep, faint boot path and descend the talus to Early Winters Creek, crossing on logs. Climb the far side on the climber's path, switchbacking up talus benches and loose cairned gullies through timber and boulders; where the boot track braids, stay climber's-left, keeping north of the drainage coming down from the basin below the spires, and aim for the obvious notch of the col. It is about 3,500 ft of gain and 3-4 hours with an overnight pack, and snow can linger in the gully below the col into July, so carry an axe early in the season.

waypoints.name: Chianti Spire / East Face (Rebel Yell) area
waypoints.directions: Drop off the col down a short snow and rock step and traverse south beneath the east face of Burgundy Spire, crossing a small snowy rib onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, then around to the obvious east side of Chianti Spire at about 7,900 ft. Reckon on under an hour from the col, or from the larch bench camp lower down. Carry an ice axe through midsummer, as the rib and the glacier margin are often firm or icy first thing in the morning.

waypoints.name: Chianti Spire Summit

before.overview: Chianti Spire is the second Wine Spire north of Silver Star's summit, standing between Burgundy Spire (north) and Pernod/Chablis (south). Its East Face carries the area's best-known moderate testpiece, commonly called 'East Face' or 'Rebel Yell' — a sustained, 6-to-7-pitch splitter crack climb (depending on which start you take) through every crack size from fingers to offwidth, finishing on an exposed summit block. It shares the same long, steep Burgundy Col approach and rappel descent as the rest of the Wine Spires, and is often linked with Burgundy or Pernod Spire on a multi-summit day.
before.beta: Rebel Yell is a well-established North Cascades classic featuring 7 pitches of alpine trad climbing (5.10 overall with the 5.10b crux on P5). The route climbs the clean east face via splitter cracks with varied techniques. All pitches are led on gear. Descent via 4 double-rope rappels on fixed anchors. Extra gear can be cached at base. Typically done as 2-day expedition.
before.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround given approach length and rappel descent.
before.rappels: Rappel the route on fixed anchors, generally trending climber's right; two 60m ropes recommended. Parties describe roughly 4 double-rope rappels from the summit block back to the base (first from the summit block, second from the top of the P5 crux pitch, remaining down slabby terrain to the glacier/snow).
before.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
before.comms: No cell service at Washington Pass or on the Burgundy Col approach; a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is strongly recommended. Closest services are in Winthrop or Mazama, WA (Methow Valley).
before.descent: Rappel the standard descent line off the spire.
obj_haz: glacier/snow crossing on approach (ice axe, sometimes crampons)

before.pro_needs: Solid alpine trad rack with doubles through offwidth sizes (#0.75-#3); comfort placing and evaluating gear in wide cracks and on fixed rappel anchors.
before.best_season: Late June/July through September; the approach gully below Burgundy Col often holds snow into July, so most parties find the driest, most straightforward conditions in August-September.
before.approach: This is the same East Face/Rebel Yell line as wa_east_face_rebel_yell, so the hike-in is identical. From the SR-20 pullout near milepost ~166 (~0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff), a steep, faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek; cross the creek and follow the climber's path/talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col — roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. Stay climber's-left toward the obvious col notch where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down. A snow patch at/near the col is the last dependable water source but is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer. From Burgundy Col, drop a short snow/rock step and traverse south below Burgundy Spire's East Face, across a small snowy rib, onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, and around to Chianti Spire's obvious east side and the base of the route (~7,900 ft) — under an hour from a col or Larch Bench camp. Carry an ice axe for this traverse through midsummer; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning.
before.descent_text: Same descent as the standard East Face/Rebel Yell line: rappel back down the route itself on fixed anchors rather than walking off. The usual descent is four double-rope rappels using two ropes (a single 60m may work for some stations but isn't the norm), starting from the summit block, then anchors near the top of pitch 5, then continuing stations down the route generally trending climber's-right. Anchors are fixed but should be visually checked each time — this isn't a heavily-bolted sport-style descent. Rope-snag hazard exists in the chimney/offwidth pitches. After reaching the base, reverse the Silver Star Glacier traverse and snow step back to Burgundy Col, then descend the climber's trail to Early Winters Creek and the highway — parties describe this exit as notably long and tiring relative to the climb, so plan daylight accordingly.
before.bail: Rappel from any belay if forced to retreat.

pitch_detail.notes: Flakes and a crack lead up into the route's obvious wide dihedral; the easier right-hand start (wider crack) joins here, while the harder left-start finger-crack variation (5.10b, with a chimney exit) rejoins by the top of this pitch. Protects well despite the width.

pitch_detail.belay: A small stance just above the offwidth, with a horizontal crack to stand on.
pitch_detail.notes: Short fist crack widens into true offwidth; using face holds outside the crack makes it feel easier than it looks from below. Belay from a stance on a horizontal break (parties on the harder left-start variation rate this pitch 5.9+/10b).

pitch_detail.belay: A slung block on the right in the dihedral, about 30 feet under the headwall, before the route pushes left.
pitch_detail.notes: Easier face-and-flake climbing up a lower-angle dihedral; a slung block provides a natural belay. Strong parties often link this with pitch 2 as one long block.

pitch_detail.belay: A sloping ledge reached by moving left on good cracks, directly under the steep thin-hands crack.
pitch_detail.notes: Cracks lead to a balancy, low-friction blind step left across an arete, protected by a single fixed bolt, gaining a sloping stance below the steep splitter above.

pitch_detail.belay: A small ledge with a bolted anchor at the top of the crack, under the last offwidth section.
pitch_detail.notes: The technical crux: a sustained, steep thin-hands crack widening through cupped hands to fists, capped by a short strenuous offwidth move, to a bolted belay stance that doubles as a rappel anchor. Bring doubles from #0.75 to #3.5 to cover the full size range.

Continues the same crack system through wide hands and offwidth in a shallow dihedral, then a rising ramp trends left to the base of the exposed summit block. Watch for rope drag/snag risk through the wider sections.
Short, exposed final moves on good holds gain the summit block, passing a single fixed bolt that also serves as the first of four double-rope rappel anchors used to descend the route.

days.note: Same approach used for Silver Star Mountain: forest trail from the Hwy 20 pullout, a creek crossing, then steep, loose, cairned gullies to the 6,600 ft bench and up to the bivy sites at Burgundy Col. Snow patches near the col usually supply water, but they can be gone or rock-hard late in a dry season. Budget 3-5 hours depending on load and fitness.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).

overnight_permit.where: Camping at Burgundy Col and the approach benches needs no permit; Lone Fir Campground is a fee, first-come first-served car campground, not a backcountry permit area.

road.driveNote: Trailhead pullout is near milepost ~166 on SR-20, about 4 miles east of Washington Pass - about 2.8 miles east of the highway's hairpin turn and 0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff. Confirm current SR-20 status with WSDOT before traveling.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 typically closes in November and reopens between mid-April and late June depending on snowpack and any storm/slide repair work (opening dates have ranged as late as mid-June in heavy-snow years).

climate.typical: Drier east-slope alpine climate; afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and snow can linger in the Burgundy Col approach gully into July.

bySeason.fall: Good climbing early, then increasing snow and eventual highway closure by November.
bySeason.spring: Approach still holds snow; SR-20 may still be closed over the pass.
bySeason.summer: Prime alpine rock season, especially August-September once the approach gully has melted out; watch for afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Highway closed, full winter/avalanche conditions — not a climbing season for this route.

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service (based in Winthrop) provides local ambulance/EMS response for the Methow Valley; for SAR call 911 first.
emergency.county: Okanogan (confirmed — Silver Star Mountain and the Wine Spires ridge lie entirely within Okanogan County, WA).
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest), Winthrop, WA.
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster, WA (~60 miles via SR-20 and Hwy 153, roughly 1.5 hrs drive from the trailhead); Mid-Valley Hospital in Omak is a second option.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency/SAR dispatch (509) 422-7232.

crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 10-25 parties per summer - a known and widely praised Wine Spires classic but the long approach and bivy/2-day commitment keep it well below trade-route traffic

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong approach fitness - steep off-trail talus and a climber's trail up to Burgundy Col with real elevation gain before any climbing begins; many parties break the day into a 2-day trip with a high camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight alpine rack plus bivy gear if camping at Burgundy Col/Larch Bench (typical 30-40 lb approach pack); lighter if attempting car-to-car

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - talus and climber's-trail approach to Burgundy Col is a significant undertaking on its own; frequently done as an overnight rather than a single big car-to-car day

partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine trad leader comfortable running it out on featured granite; should have prior multi-pitch alpine rock and rappel-descent experience, ideally in the Washington Pass / Wine Spires area or similar committing granite towers

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September - this matches the drier east-slope alpine window before the pass closes for winter

July.reason: Prime alpine rock season; snow largely cleared from approach by mid-July, though early-month lingering snow patches possible

August.reason: Driest, most stable month; typical prime window for the Wine Spires

September.reason: Still good rock season but shorter days and higher chance of an early-season storm cycle as fall approaches; watch for highway closure risk creeping in late in the month

weather.typical: Drier east-slope alpine climate; expect warm, mostly stable summer days with cooler nights at the Burgundy Col camp
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer - start early (with the 5:00 AM start from camp) to be off the exposed upper pitches before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained, committing exposure typical of a Grade III alpine tower - seven pitches with exposed belays; loose rock in spots adds objective hazard, and retreat from upper pitches requires multiple rappels rather than a simple walk-off, so a stuck party or weather change mid-route is a real consequence

avalanche.zone: N/A - summer rock route; nearest NWAC coverage is the East Slopes Central zone, but that forecast is not maintained during the July-September dry-rock climbing season for this route

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Beyond Burgundy Col the standard approach crosses a section of the upper Silver Star Glacier to reach Chianti Spire's east side; conditions vary by season from an easy unroped snow slog to requiring a rope, so carry an axe and assess crevasse conditions before crossing.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then the snow traverse south beneath Burgundy's east face onto the Silver Star Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, a steep faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek. Cross the creek and follow the climber's path and talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col, roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. Stay climber's-left toward the obvious col notch where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down.

A snow patch at or near the col is the last dependable water and is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer.
hazards: A snow and glacier traverse that can be firm or icy in the morning; carry an axe through midsummer
The last dependable water is a snow patch at the col which is unreliable by late summer
Rope-snag hazard in the chimney and offwidth pitches on the rappel descent
Fixed anchors that should be visually checked at each station; this is not a bolted sport descent
A re-ascent of 200-300 ft back to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Burgundy Col, drop a short snow and rock step and traverse south beneath Burgundy Spire's East Face, across a small snowy rib, onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, and around to Chianti Spire's obvious east side at about 7,900 ft. Under an hour from a col or bench camp.

So the sequence of surfaces is the handrail, and you can feel each one underfoot: rock step down, snow traverse, a rib, then glacier. If you have not crossed onto glacier you have not gone far enough.

The route on the face, and this is where the two east-face lines are told apart: Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face. Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. So: a big corner on the right-hand side of the wall is this route. A ramp under the summit that leans left is not.

Confirm on the climb: seven pitches at III 5.10b, with chimney and offwidth pitches that readily snag ropes on the way down. Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes get you back down the route itself, trending generally climber's-right, starting from the summit block and then anchors near the top of pitch 5.

What going too far looks like on the approach: continuing south past Chianti along the glacier brings you under Pernod and toward the Pernod-Chablis notch, which serves different routes and involves loose fourth-class ground.

An ice axe is wanted for this traverse through midsummer; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning, and that is exactly when you will be crossing them.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

before.name: Lichen Bouquet (East Face)
before.fa: Alan Kearney, John Culberson, and Shaun Kelley, September 8, 1989
gear: Doubles of cams from finger size through #3 Camalot
One #3.5 or #4 Camalot for the offwidth
8-10 alpine draws plus several double-length slings for the ramp
Cordelette or long slings for belays
Rock shoes plus approach shoes or light boots
hazards: Rockfall in the cairned approach gullies below Burgundy Col.
Loose and lichenous rock on a seldom-repeated alpine face.
Steep snow and open moats on the descent from the col and on the year-round traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face.
Stuck ropes on flake and offwidth features during a rappel descent of the east face.
Convective summer thunderstorms with lightning exposure on an isolated granite spire.
Sand-over-slab footing on the descent above the 6,400-6,600 ft bench.
A committing evacuation - roughly 3.5 miles and 3,700 ft of steep, loose ground back to SR 20, in a drainage with no cell coverage.
High water in Early Winters Creek during spring melt at the log crossing.
before.overview: A 5.9 line on the same east face as Rebel Yell, following a long left-leaning ramp into a left-facing corner and an offwidth, then crossing Rebel Yell and continuing to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, where a short pitch on the normal route reaches the summit.
before.beta: Established in 1989, this is the second-best-known line on Chianti's east face and a quieter alternative to Rebel Yell at a full grade easier. It starts directly below the summit, following a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an off-width crack; three more pitches cross Rebel Yell and gain the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, and a short pitch reaches the summit up the normal route. Approach and descent logistics are identical to Rebel Yell - the same Early Winters Creek trail to Burgundy Col, the same drop and traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and a rappel-based descent. It is graded II 5.9 or III 5.9. Detail is thin: pitch lengths and total footage are not known, so this is a route for a party comfortable route-finding on an alpine face rather than following a topo.
before.turnaround: Set a turnaround before you leave the ground and hold to it. With little known detail and route-finding that crosses another established line, this route swallows time - judge progress against a fixed clock rather than against feeling close to the top. Both bracketing hazards, the snow traverse under Burgundy Spire and the loose gully below the col, want daylight and firm snow, and summer thunderstorms build fast over the Silver Star cirque with no shelter available on the spire.
before.rappels: 4 double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes down the neighbouring Rebel Yell line, from the two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block; or reverse to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
before.comms: No usable cell coverage should be assumed. The approach drops into the roadless Early Winters Creek drainage, and both the bench camp and Burgundy Col sit away from the highway corridor; SR 20 itself has long dead zones over Washington Pass. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB.
before.descent: Descend from the summit toward the Burgundy-Chianti notch, or rappel the neighbouring Rebel Yell line with two 60 m ropes, then reverse the snow traverse to Burgundy Col and the approach trail.

timing.recommendedStart: From Burgundy Col, first light. From the 6,400-6,600 ft bench, about 90 minutes before first light. Car-to-car, leave the SR 20 pullout well before dawn. With sparse beta and likely route-finding delays, start earlier than you would for Rebel Yell.

before.detailed_rack: No published rack exists for this specific line, so carry the standard Chianti east-face kit: a set of nuts, doubles of cams from finger size through #3 Camalot, and a #3.5 or #4 Camalot for the offwidth the first-ascent party describes low on the route. Add 8-10 alpine draws and several double-length slings for the long left-leaning ramp, which will generate rope drag. Two 60 m ropes are essential for the descent and for the option of escaping onto Rebel Yell's rappel line.
what_to_bring: Trekking poles for the steep sandy approach and descent
2-3 L water capacity - the bench spring and snow at Burgundy Col are the only sources
Satellite messenger or PLB
Headlamp with fresh batteries
Long sleeves and trousers for the offwidth and lichen
Sunglasses, sun hat, high-SPF sunscreen for snow glare
Wind shell and a light insulating layer
Gaiters for scree and snow
Bivy or camping kit if overnighting; stove to melt snow at the col
Map and compass or GPS on the Silver Star Mountain quad
First-aid and blister kit
A photo of the east face taken from the approach traverse to help identify the ramp
ice axe and crampons — approach traverse
pro_tips: Little detail is known - treat this as a route-finding exercise on an alpine face, not a topo climb, and study the east face on the approach traverse.

The line starts directly below the summit and leans left, whereas Rebel Yell takes the obvious dihedral on the right side of the face; that contrast is the easiest way to tell them apart from the snow.
Because you cross Rebel Yell partway up, that route's fixed anchors are your escape hatch - knowing where they are before you start is worth the reading.
Expect more lichen than on Rebel Yell; the name is not decorative, and the rock sees far less traffic.
Extend runners generously on the long left-leaning ramp to keep rope drag manageable.
The first-ascent partners are given as either Kearney, Culberson and Kelley or Kearney and Houston, and the commitment grade as either II or III.
Leave boots, axe, crampons and poles at the base if you intend to descend by rappelling back to the same spot.
watch_out: Route-finding is the real difficulty: the line crosses Rebel Yell and the published description is a single paragraph.
Lichen-covered, infrequently travelled rock means poorer friction and a higher chance of loose holds than on the neighbouring classic.
The offwidth low on the route needs a large cam and wide-crack technique.
The 200-300 ft descent off the south side of Burgundy Col is steep snow early, moats mid-season and loose rock late.
Snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face persists year-round - axe and crampons are needed all season.
Afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque leave nowhere to shelter.
The sandy slab descent above the bench is slippery and is where most parties take falls.
before.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad protection on granite: ramps, a left-facing corner and an offwidth, with no fixed gear reported on the line itself. The offwidth section will want at least one large cam. Because the route crosses Rebel Yell, the fixed anchors on that line (bolts at the top of P4 and at both ends of the P5 offwidth, plus the two-bolt station at the base of the summit block) are usable for retreat. Expect more lichen and less-travelled rock than on Rebel Yell - the route's name is a fair warning - so protect for the possibility of a loose hold.
before.best_season: Late June through late September, matching the rest of the Wine Spires, with July to mid-September most reliable. The spire's seasons are summer and fall. Early season means continuous snow in the col gully (better travel, but axe and crampons mandatory) and possibly wet rock in the corner systems; by August the rock is dry but the gully is sand-over-slab and the moats along the traverse are open. September gives the most stable weather and quietest conditions, offset by short days and a cold east face that only catches morning sun. Nothing is accessible once SR 20 closes for the winter.
before.approach: Identical to Rebel Yell. Drive SR 20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166, at roughly 4,250 ft (about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road, about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn). No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder. Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft - the standard low camp, with a year-round spring about 200 yards north of the trail and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above. Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours. From the col, descend 200-300 ft on the south side and traverse right beneath Burgundy Spire's east face on year-round snow with seasonal rock bands until Chianti's east face is in view. Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face; Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. Under an hour from the col.
before.descent_text: Most parties on the east face descend the way Rebel Yell parties do: from the summit pedestal, scramble to the two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block and make four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow at the base of the face, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling the ropes carefully - the flake and offwidth features snag ropes readily. The alternative, and the one this route's finish naturally suggests, is to reverse to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti and descend from there. Either way, collect gear left at the base, reverse the snow traverse north beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col - much easier on firm snow than late-day slush or bare sand. Then descend the loose main gully (helmets on), rejoin the trail at the bench, and take the steep path down to Early Winters Creek, finishing with the short loose scramble back up to the highway. The sandy slabs above the bench are the most-cursed section of the whole outing; trekking poles help.
before.bail: Retreat is by rappel with two 60 m ropes. Because the route crosses Rebel Yell partway up, a party that gets stopped can traverse to Rebel Yell's fixed anchors (top of P4, top of P5, and the two-bolt station at the southeast base of the summit block) and rappel that line back to the base - the most reliable escape from anywhere high on the east face. Below the climb, the only exit is the approach in reverse over the snow traverse and back up to Burgundy Col; if the traverse snow is hard and you have no crampons, bail at the col instead.

pitch_detail.notes: Begins directly below the summit; follow a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an offwidth crack. No pitch lengths are published for this route.
Three more pitches lead up, crossing Rebel Yell, and finally gain the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti. Rebel Yell's fixed anchors are encountered en route and serve as a retreat option.
A short pitch leads to the summit up the normal route - i.e. the 1952 North Face finish from the Burgundy-Chianti notch, topping out on the chossy summit block with its old bolt.

before.itinerary: Two-day: Day 1, hike from SR 20 to the 6,400-6,600 ft bench or Burgundy Col (3-4 hours to the col), optionally climbing a second Wine Spires objective such as Burgundy Spire's North Face (5.8) or Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge (5.8+). Day 2, traverse from the col to Chianti's east face, climb Lichen Bouquet, descend, regain the col and hike out. A fit party can do it car-to-car in a long day, as parties routinely do on the neighbouring Rebel Yell, but how little is known about this line argues for the extra time.

access.fees: None - no day-use or climbing fee; highway-shoulder parking is free.
access.permit: No climbing permit and no overnight permit are required. Standard Leave No Trace practice applies.
access.closures: Seasonal only: SR 20 over Washington Pass closes with sustained winter snow (typically November or December) and reopens in spring. WSDOT has also closed sections mid-season for storm and rockslide repairs, as in 2026.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan County, Washington. The surrounding designation is given as the North Cascades Scenic Highway corridor.
access.passRequired: None. A Northwest Forest Pass is specifically NOT required, because parking is on the state highway shoulder rather than at a Forest Service trailhead.

road.name: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway / Washington Pass)
road.status: Paved two-lane state highway suitable for any passenger car; parking on the highway shoulder at a wide pullout near milepost 166. No forest-road driving involved.
road.driveNote: From Washington Pass drive about 4 miles east to a broad pullout on the south (right) side of the highway near milepost 166, at roughly 4,250 ft, directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain - about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road and about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn. Several smaller pullouts come first. From the east, a short drive up-valley from Mazama and Early Winters.
road.seasonalGate: WSDOT closes SR 20 across Washington Pass each winter and reopens it in spring after avalanche control and snow clearing. Dates vary widely; in 2026 the full highway did not reopen until 14 June after emergency storm and rockslide repairs - the latest since 1974 - with the eastern portion open from 30 April. Check WSDOT before driving.

climate.fall: September into early October brings the most stable weather of the year, cool climbing, quiet trails and larches at the bench camp - offset by short days, a cold east face with only morning sun, and open moats at the snow-rock margin.
climate.spring: Out of season. SR 20 is typically gated, the approach gully and traverse are full snow travel with avalanche potential, and the east face is cold and often damp in the corner systems.
climate.summer: The season. Late June through August gives dry cracks and long days, though the col gully holds snow into early summer and the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face carries snow year-round. Early starts are essential for firm snow and for beating afternoon convection.
climate.winter: Access is closed with SR 20; the approach is avalanche terrain and the route is not a realistic winter objective.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope Cascade climate in the crest's rain shadow - fast-drying rock and frequent settled high pressure, with clear mornings that often build into afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque.
climate.forecastZone: Okanogan County, eastern North Cascades. Use the NOAA/NWS point forecast for Washington Pass and the Northwest Avalanche Center's Washington Pass and Mazama weather stations for shoulder-season snow information; elevation-band forecasts for Silver Star Mountain cover the same cirque.

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service provides EMS and transport in the Methow Valley. Evacuation from the east face means rappelling, reversing the snow traverse, regaining Burgundy Col and carrying roughly 3.5 miles and 3,700 ft down to SR 20. Leave a written plan with someone off the mountain and carry a satellite messenger.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, 24 West Chewuch Road, Winthrop, WA 98862 - 509-996-4000 (Mon-Fri, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.). An older district number is 509-996-2266.
emergency.nearestHospital: Mid-Valley Hospital, 810 Jasmine Street, Omak, WA 98841 - 509-826-1760, roughly 30 miles from Winthrop. Three Rivers Hospital, 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA 98812 - 509-689-2517, a similar distance. There is no hospital in Winthrop or Mazama.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies. Okanogan County Sheriff / 911 Dispatch Center non-emergency line: 509-422-7232 (or 800-572-6604 from within area code 509). Okanogan County Search and Rescue responds only to assignments from the Sheriff's Office; Sheriff's Office main line 509-422-7200.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the east-face corners have dried and the col gully is still easy to travel

July.reason: Snow in the gully below Burgundy Col eases travel while the east face dries; moats begin opening along the traverse.

June.reason: SR 20 is open by now but the col gully is full snow needing axe and crampons, and the east-face corners may still seep.

August.reason: Dry rock in the corner systems; the gully becomes sand over slab and moats on the traverse open wider, so plan the descent.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the lichenous rock and the highway nearing its winter closure leave little margin.

September.reason: Stable weather and quiet, but short days and a cold east face that loses the sun by midday make the 5.9 pitches chilly.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 4 on two 60 m ropes, trending to the rappeller's right.
rappel_detail.anchor: two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block
hazards: Check the fixed anchor before weighting it.
rappel_detail.station: The southeast base of the summit block, reached by scrambling down from the summit pedestal.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull carefully: the flake and offwidth features snag ropes readily.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 4 on two ropes, continuing to the right.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed anchor at the top of the pitch-5 crux
hazards: Rope snags in the chimney and offwidth sections.
rappel_detail.station: The top of the crux fifth pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 4 on two ropes down slabby terrain.
rappel_detail.station: A fixed station lower on the face, on the slabbier ground to climber's right of the route.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 4 of 4, to the snow at the base of the face; collect any gear left there and reverse the snow traverse to Burgundy Col.
rappel_detail.station: The lowest fixed station on the face.

before.rappel_count_note: Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes from the summit block back to the snow, trending to the rappeller's right. A single 60 m rope may reach some stations but is not the norm. Individual lengths are not published.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout, the bench camp and the main gully to Burgundy Col, then south on year-round snow to the ramp below the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166 at roughly 4,250 ft, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road and about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn. No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder.

Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft, the standard low camp. There is a year-round spring about 200 yards north of the trail at the bench, and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above.

Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours.
hazards: A roughly 40-degree snow finger in the main gully below the col into midsummer
Year-round snow on the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face, with seasonal rock bands
Rope-snagging flake and offwidth features on the rappel descent
A 200-300 ft re-ascent to the col at the end of the day
Sand-over-slab above the bench, described by trip reports as the worst part of the outing
Rockfall from parties above in the gullies; keep helmets on
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. That is the test, and it is both positional and directional: stand where the summit is straight above you, and look for a ramp that leans left.

The negative test is the other line on the same face, and they are genuinely easy to confuse from below: Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face. If you are under a big corner on the right-hand side of the wall rather than a left-leaning ramp under the top, you are on Rebel Yell.

Getting there: from Burgundy Col, descend 200-300 ft on the south side and traverse right beneath Burgundy Spire's East Face on year-round snow, with seasonal rock bands, until Chianti's East Face is in view. Under an hour from the col.

So the snow is the handrail and it is there all year, which is unusual and useful: if you are not walking on snow beneath a big east-facing wall, you have not started the traverse.

Descent, and the route's own finish suggests the alternative: most east-face parties descend as Rebel Yell parties do, scrambling from the summit pedestal to a two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block and making four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling ropes carefully, since the flake and offwidth features snag readily. The alternative this route's finish naturally suggests is to reverse to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti and descend from there.

The sting in the tail, which is a timing decision made at the base: whichever way you come down, you must regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col, and that is much easier on firm morning snow than on late-day slush or bare sand.

before.name: North Face (Original Route, 1952)
before.fa: Joe Hieb and Art Maki, September 1952 (first ascent of the spire)
gear: Single rack of cams roughly 0.4-3 inches
6-8 alpine draws plus two double-length slings
Cordelette or 120 cm slings for anchors
hazards: Loose, unstable rock reported on two leads by the first-ascent party.
before.overview: The original 1952 first-ascent line up Chianti Spire, gained by rappelling into the Burgundy-Chianti notch and climbing the peak's north side on then-loose rock; now rarely repeated in favor of the East Face/Rebel Yell.
before.beta: First ascensionists Joe Hieb and Art Maki approached via moraine and ice to the eastern walls of the Wine Spires group, made a roughly 250-ft rappel off the west face into the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires, and found the north face held the only route to the top. Two leads of unstable rock presented the main difficulties, protected with seven pitons for aid/safety, and the final moves to the tiny summit required a shoulder-stand and flipping the rope over a rock flake.
before.turnaround: Fix a turnaround time before you leave camp and honour it. The day's crux for safety is not the 5.6 climbing but the snow traverse and the loose gully below Burgundy Col, both of which want daylight and firm snow - plan to be back at the col well before the afternoon softens things. Summer thunderstorms build quickly over the Silver Star cirque and the spires are lightning-exposed with no shelter; if towers are forming, retreat rather than continue to the summit block.
before.rappels: 1 short rappel or downclimb off the summit block, from an old bolt, then reverse the route to the Burgundy-Chianti notch; bring two ropes only if rappelling the east face instead
before.face: North face, above the Burgundy-Chianti notch
before.comms: Assume no cell coverage. The approach drops into the roadless Early Winters Creek drainage and both the bench camp and Burgundy Col are shielded from the highway corridor; SR 20 itself has long dead zones through Washington Pass. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB - the practical alternative is sending a party member down the 3,700 ft approach to the highway to flag a vehicle.
before.descent: Reverse the route to the Burgundy-Chianti notch, then reverse the snow traverse to Burgundy Col and descend the approach gully and trail.

timing.recommendedStart: From a camp at Burgundy Col, first light is enough. From the 6,400-6,600 ft bench, leave about 90 minutes before first light. Car-to-car parties leave the SR 20 pullout well before dawn - a pre-dawn start is what buys firm snow in the col gully both ways.

before.detailed_rack: A standard single alpine rack to 3 inches covers the 5.6 climbing: a set of nuts, cams from about 0.4 to 3 inches, and 6-8 alpine draws plus a couple of double-length slings for the blocky north-face features. Two 60 m ropes are the norm in the Wine Spires because every descent option in the group is rappel-based and 60 m doubles let you leave the mountain from anywhere.
what_to_bring: Trekking poles (repeatedly called the most important gear in the Wine Spires for the sandy descent)
2-3 L water capacity - the bench spring and Burgundy Col snow are the only reliable sources
Satellite messenger or PLB
Headlamp with fresh batteries
Sun hat, sunglasses and high-SPF sunscreen for snow glare
Wind/rain shell and an insulating layer for the shaded north face
Gaiters for the scree and snow
Bivy gear if camping at the col; a stove to melt snow
Map and compass or GPS with the Silver Star Mountain quad
Small first-aid kit and blister care
ice axe and aluminium crampons — col gully and the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face; on the list all season, not just in spring
pro_tips: This is the shortest technical route on the spire but the day is dominated by the 3,700 ft approach - budget your energy for the hike, not the climbing.
Do not confuse this with Burgundy Spire's North Face (5.8, 6 pitches). Most web searches for "North Face" in this cirque return Burgundy's route, which is a different climb on a different spire.
Timing the col gully for firm morning snow makes both directions dramatically easier and safer than the late-day scree slog.

The wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft is the best camp: real water, flat ground, and only about 1,500 ft below the col. Burgundy Col's two or three bivy sites are more convenient but exposed and waterless except for snow.
Carrying the ice axe and crampons to the notch and leaving them at the base of the climbing keeps you light on the fifth-class terrain.
Chianti pairs well with a second Wine Spires objective from one camp; guided programmes routinely combine a Wine Spires climb with Burgundy Spire's North Face or Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge.
watch_out: The 200-300 ft drop off the south side of Burgundy Col is the most-reported difficulty of the approach: steep snow early, deep moats mid-season, and loose rock late.
The gullies below the col are cairned but braided; parties routinely lose the line and end up on genuinely loose ground.
The summit block is chossy - the 1952 party needed a shoulder stand and a rope flip over a flake to get up it, and the modern anchor there is an old bolt.
Afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque leave no shelter anywhere on the spire or the traverse.
Snow beneath Burgundy's east face persists year-round; a party without axe and crampons can be stopped short of the climbing even in August.
Early Winters Creek can run high in spring melt; use the larger log crossing near the old cabin site rather than fording.
before.pro_needs: Historically protected with pitons; a modern ascent would rack a standard light alpine trad rack given the moderate 5.6 grade, but no contemporary route description was found to confirm current gear beta.
before.best_season: Late June through late September, with July to mid-September the reliable window. The rock dries early on this side of the range because the Wine Spires sit in the drier east-slope Cascade rain shadow, but the approach gully below Burgundy Col holds snow into early summer and the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face carries snow year-round. Early season means an ice axe and crampons are genuinely needed and the approach is arguably nicer on snow than on the summer scree; late season means dry rock, thin moats and a miserable sandy descent. September often gives the most stable weather of the year but short days and a cold, shaded north face. The route is out of the question once SR 20 closes for the winter.
before.approach: Reached from the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires (gained via a rappel from the west side per the original account, or by traversing in from Burgundy Col), then climbing the north face directly to the summit.
before.descent_text: Downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block back onto the north face, then reverse the line to the Burgundy-Chianti notch. From the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col - this re-ascent is the sting in the tail and is much easier on firm morning snow than on afternoon slush or bare, sandy rock. From the col, descend the main gully carefully; below the bench the trail is fast but relentlessly steep, and the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway is a short, loose scramble on scree and boulders. Trip reports are unanimous that the sand-over-slab descent above the bench is the worst part of the day; trekking poles help enormously, and a helmet should stay on because parties above you dislodge rocks in the gullies.
before.bail: Retreat is straightforward: the route is short and the Burgundy-Chianti notch is only a rope length or so below the summit, so a single rappel or a downclimb puts you back on the traverse at any point. The real bail decision is lower down - if the snow beneath Burgundy's east face is hard and you have no crampons, or the col gully is running with rockfall, turn around at Burgundy Col rather than committing to the traverse. Below the col, retreat is simply the approach in reverse; there is no alternative exit from the Silver Star cirque that does not involve a much longer day.

pitch_detail.notes: From Burgundy Col, descend 200-300 ft, traverse south on year-round snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, then work up broken ground to the notch between Burgundy and Chianti. Axe and crampons useful all season.

Short fifth-class climbing on the north side directly above the notch. Beckey rates the route II 5.6 overall; a 1990 account of a neighbouring east-face line describes the finish from this notch as a short pitch up the normal route. No source publishes a footage figure.
pitch_detail.pitch: North face to the summit pedestal

before.itinerary: Most parties treat this as a two-day trip. Day 1: hike from the SR 20 pullout to the 6,400-6,600 ft bench (good camping, water) or push on to one of the two or three bivy sites at Burgundy Col (year-round snow for water, austere and exposed); 3-4 hours to the col. Day 2: traverse from the col to the Burgundy-Chianti notch, climb the North Face to the summit, reverse to the col and hike out. Fit parties climb Chianti car-to-car in a long day, and the North Face pairs naturally with a second Wine Spires objective - Burgundy Spire's North Face (5.8) or Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge (5.8+) - from the same camp.

Always check WSDOT's North Cascades Highway page before driving from either side.

climate.fall: September into early October is often the most stable and pleasant window - cool, dry air and firm ground - at the cost of short days, cold shade on the north side, and thin, melted-out snow with wide moats at the rock margin.
climate.spring: Snow-covered and generally out of season. SR 20 is usually still closed; when it opens, the approach gully to Burgundy Col and the traverse under Burgundy's east face are full winter/spring snow travel with avalanche potential, and the rock routes are wet and cold.
climate.summer: The season. Late June through August gives warm, mostly dry days, though the approach gully holds snow into early summer and the traverse under Burgundy Spire carries snow year-round. Start early to be off the exposed summit before afternoon convection and to catch the col gully while the snow is firm.
climate.winter: SR 20 is gated closed across Washington Pass, removing practical access. The approach gully below Burgundy Col is avalanche terrain and the spires are not a realistic winter objective from this side.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope Cascade climate. The Wine Spires sit far enough east of the crest to escape much of the maritime weather that plagues the western North Cascades, so the rock dries fast and settled high-pressure spells are common. The dominant summer hazard is convective: clear mornings that build into afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque.
climate.forecastZone: Okanogan County, eastern North Cascades. emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service provides EMS and transport in the Methow Valley. approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself. The original party approached from a camp at the head of Silver Star Creek, climbed 500 ft of difficult rock to the notch between Chianti and Pernod, made a 250 ft rappel on the west face, and followed a loose gully to the Chianti-Burgundy notch, where the north face was found to hold the only route.
hazards: A 200-300 ft re-ascent to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
Loose main gully below the col, with rockfall from parties above
Sand-over-slab descent above the bench, unanimously described as the worst part of the day
A short loose scramble on scree and boulders for the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway
A route with a single detailed historical account and little modern traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the notch between Chianti and Burgundy spires, and the modern way in is to traverse to it from Burgundy Col rather than to rappel into it from the west as the first ascent did. From the notch, the north face is climbed directly to the summit.

So the test is that you are in a gap between two named spires with a wall rising north of you. Burgundy on one side, Chianti on the other, and the face you are about to climb between them.

The discriminator against the peak's other lines, and it is a side-of-the-spire test: the two East Face routes are reached by descending 200-300 ft south from Burgundy Col and traversing on snow beneath Burgundy's east face until Chianti's east face comes into view. This route stops short of that, at the notch. If you are standing on snow looking at a big east-facing wall with a dihedral on its right side, you have gone past the notch and are under Rebel Yell.

And the other notch on this spire is the one at the far end: the first ascent reached the Chianti-Pernod notch first, on the other side of the peak, and had to rappel 250 ft off the west face and follow a loose gully to get to this one. Two notches, one at each end of Chianti. This route uses the Burgundy end.

What coming back looks like, and it is the same sting the East Face routes carry: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block onto the north face, reverse the line to the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col. Firm morning snow makes that far easier than afternoon slush or bare sandy rock.

expect.approach: The North Fork Sauk approach starts from the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers'-trail pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road, reached via SR 530 south of Darrington) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk River — not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649, but a boot path a short distance further along FR 49. From the pullout the path is flat and brushy (stinging nettle, then devil's club) for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the North Fork Sauk River, which must be forded or crossed on logs (log jams are usually adequate about 0.5 mi in; they shift year to year and can be dicey in high water/early season). The path fords the river braids two to three times over the next mile, then follows Cougar Creek upstream on a faint, cairned/flagged track through sandy streambed and forest — expect route-finding to be slow here, especially with snow on the ground into early summer. Around 3,000–3,200 ft the trail crosses Cougar Creek itself (can be impassable lower down; look for a crossing around 3.2K ft) and climbs steeply through switchbacks in forest, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft (roughly 2–2.5 hrs from the car, and the last reliable water before the basin). Above the falls the climbers' path breaks out of the trees onto scree and slabs, angling up to the 5,800 ft saddle/basin on Sloan's northeast side (reached ~4–5 hrs in for most parties), with a small stream and possible campsite in the basin — the standard overnight/base camp spot for a two-day ascent. From the basin, ledges and slabs lead up to the toe of the Sloan Glacier; rope up and gear up (crampons, axe, glacier kit) here before crossing onto the ice toward the southeast edge of the summit massif. The often-preferred approach uses the Bedal Creek trailhead (FS 4096, a rough 3-mile 4WD spur off the Mountain Loop Highway, ~2,790 ft) and the old Bedal Creek trail/climbers' path to the same 5,300 ft Bedal–Sloan saddle, avoiding the North Fork Sauk fords entirely at the cost of a rougher access road; total stats by that line run about 9.5 mi and 5,300 ft round trip. Either way, expect avalanche/snow-slope hazard on the basin and glacier approach into early summer, one notable open crevasse on the Sloan Glacier that's typically snow-bridged in normal season, and generally loose, brushy, unmaintained tread below treeline on both approaches. Most parties now come in by the Bedal Creek trail instead: the road up to it is potholed with one washed-out stretch near the top, so bring high clearance, and from the upper parking head straight into the forest rather than up the logging spur to the right (in early July the first mile is choked with blowdown and brush).

set.approach: Most parties start from the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,800 ft, at the end of a rough high-clearance spur (Forest Road 4096) off the Mountain Loop Highway a mile or so past the Bedal campground. Follow the Bedal Creek trail through old-growth forest and along the creek to where a large washout has taken the tread; scramble the washout to a cairned exit, then climb the climbers' path through forest and onto talus and meadow to the saddle near 5,300 ft, the last dependable water. From there bear toward the moraine and the lower glacier. A second, less used approach starts from the pullout on Sloan Creek Road and fords the North Fork Sauk River, then follows Cougar Creek; it avoids the Bedal road, but the crossings are dangerous in high water, mainly May through July.

before.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the short, low-5th-class/exposed Class 4 step about 100 ft below the true summit (the 'bear hug' move on the ridge has solid hand cracks on both sides and is usually downclimbed free by competent parties). Parties uncomfortable downclimbing it can rig a short hand line or single-strand rappel here — there is no fixed/bolted anchor; build off a rock horn, chockstone, or gear placement, and a single 30 m/60 m rope doubled is more than enough for the ~15-20 ft of steep rock involved. Below that, follow cairns and the climbers' trail back along the south-face heather ledges and the loose scree/dirt gully that gained access from the ledge system — this gully is notably loose underfoot and the ledges above it have real exposure (parties have noted a ~500 ft unprotected drop at the outer edge), so downclimb it carefully rather than glissading or rushing. At the base of the gully/ledges, re-rope for the glacier crossing back to the toe where gear was staged, then continue down slabs to the basin/saddle. From there it's a full reversal of whichever approach was used — steep scree/slab and forest switchbacks back to the Cougar Creek waterfall and North Fork Sauk crossings (Sloan Creek/FR 49 approach), or the Bedal Creek climbers' path and old trail (Bedal Creek/FS 4096 approach) — down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no standard rappelling on the glacier or ledges; the only rope use besides glacier travel is the optional short hand line/rappel off the summit step described above. bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your right for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
approach_variants.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.

approach_variants.whyThisWay: Later in July and August when the river is low, or when the rough spur to the Bedal trailhead is impassable; the traditional approach, but with log crossings and brushy tread.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your right, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

climbing_route.label: Glacier exit onto the east rock
climbing_route.notes: Head southwest across the glacier toward the obvious corner where the left skyline of the summit massif meets the east ridge, staying high and right on the glacier and then angling left to within about 100 ft of the east rock face. The face above sheds rock, so move left if debris is coming down and do not linger under it. Leaving the snow for rock near 7,100 ft is where the route gets awkward late in the season — the moat opens and crevasses lower on the slope may force a detour to a lower crossing. Glacier gear can be left at this transition.

climbing_route.label: Heather shelf across the south face
climbing_route.notes: The corkscrew itself: a rock-and-heather shelf carrying a well-worn goat and climber path that cuts high across the entire south face, around the corner and partway onto the west face. The tread is good and the scrambling easy, but above roughly 7,200 ft the ledge is edged by a drop of around 500 ft, so this is the section where a slip is not survivable despite the modest grade. Wet or frosted heather and lingering snow patches on the shelf are the thing to watch.

climbing_route.label: Summit gully to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: A prominent gully at the far end of the traverse is climbed straight up to its top at the ridge crest. Mostly second and third class with a few sections where hands are needed; loose material in the gully means keeping the party close together or spread out sideways.

climbing_route.label: Class 4 step and summit scramble
climbing_route.notes: At the crest move east (left) just below the ridge, climb a short steep step of about class 4, then scramble a further 200-300 ft of exposed third class on granite to the summit. Descent reverses the whole line, and the corkscrew is easy to lose from above — note where the shelf leaves the ridge on the way up, because dropping off the wrong side of the south face leads into cliffs.

expect.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, downclimb the same Class 2 (right side) or Class 2/3 (center) slope back down about 600 vertical feet to the ~5,000 ft bench, then reverse the counterclockwise talus traverse below the cliff bands back to treeline, and continue down through open forest and brush to the FR-6517 parking area. No technical anchors or rappels are needed on the standard line. The main descent hazards are loose talus/scree (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below) and route-finding — in poor visibility it's easy to drift toward the cliff bands instead of holding the correct counterclockwise line, so retrace your ascent traverse carefully. Parties who climbed the more exposed far-left finish (about 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3) sometimes downclimb that section more cautiously or carry ~50 ft of rope to rig an optional handline for extra security, but this is a personal-comfort choice on a minor variation, not a fixed rappel station, and the standard Class 2/3 line requires no rope at all. Parties in September and July used a short rappel (about 15-30 m) from a tree above the cliff band, or the fixed rope found at the steep forest bypass, to get down the crux section safely.

set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. The one place that is not a plain walk-off is the lower cliff band on the north side, roughly 15 m of slabby rock and loose dirt. In dry weather it downclimbs at class 3; wet, mossy or snowy it is closer to class 4 and most parties rope it. Walk the steep forest above it, belay off a tree just above the band, and make a single rappel of about 15 m (a 30 m rope with a sling and a rappel ring covers it). Do not rely on rope or webbing left on the slope by earlier parties. Below the band, continue the talus traverse back to treeline and the road end.

before.overview: Eagle Rock is a prominent, blocky summit (5,614 ft, about 1,400 ft of prominence) on the ridge between the Beckler River and Skykomish valleys near Stevens Pass. From the FR6517 trailhead (elev. ~4,150 ft), it's roughly 0.8 miles one-way and about 1,460 ft of gain to the top — a short outing (often under 3 hours round trip) for a big, airy summit panorama over the US-2 corridor peaks, the Beckler and North Fork Skykomish drainages, and (on clear days) Glacier Peak and the Monte Cristo group. The route finishes with a Class 2–3 scramble on blocky rock.
before.beta: From a high parking area on FR6517 about 0.5 mile east of the summit, the route gains about 1,460 ft in all, finishing with roughly 600 vertical feet of open slope/talus to the top — easy class 2 if you stay to the right side, or class 2/3 up the center. Total distance is well under a mile each way, and the round trip from the car is typically under three hours. The peak sees very few visitors compared to nearby Beckler Peak and Evergreen Mountain.
before.turnaround: This is a short outing, so set your turnaround based on weather, remaining daylight for the long forest-road drive out, and terrain conditions rather than clock time — deteriorating visibility, wet/slick rock on the class 2/3 sections, or lingering snow on the upper slope in early season are the main reasons to turn back.
before.face: Northeast side, wrapping to the north side (talus approach and scramble line)
before.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
before.descent: Reverse the scramble back to the approach.

waypoints.name: FR6517 Roadside Parking
waypoints.note: Pull-off on FR6517, reached via FR6510 and FR6514 off Beckler River Road (FR65) — about 10.8 mi of gravel forest road; parking sits roughly 0.5 mi east of the summit.
waypoints.directions: From Skykomish take the Beckler River Road (FR 65) north, then follow the FR 6510 / FR 6514 / FR 6517 spur network — about 10.8 miles of gravel and dirt past the pavement — to the road end. The spurs can be rough or snow-blocked into early summer. There is no maintained trail beyond the pull-off and no water anywhere above the car, so carry all of it from here.

waypoints.name: Brush Exit / Open Forest
waypoints.note: Route leaves the roadside brush and enters open forest within a few hundred feet of the parking pull-off — head west, straight up the hillside.
waypoints.directions: Leave the road and head west-southwest, straight up the hillside. There is no trail and no cairns, so the line is picked by eye. A short push through roadside brush puts you into open timber within the first few hundred feet.

waypoints.name: Talus Below NE Cliffs
waypoints.note: A few hundred yards past the forest edge, trees give way to loose talus beneath Eagle Rock's northeast cliff band — watch for rockfall from above and unstable blocks underfoot.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing west through the timber; after a few hundred yards the trees thin and the ground turns to open talus. It is steep — nearly all of the route's roughly 1,400 ft of gain is packed into the 0.8 mile from the car, so it feels considerably bigger than the mileage suggests.

waypoints.name: Start of Counterclockwise Traverse
waypoints.note: Begin the ascending, counterclockwise traverse around the peak toward its north side; stay on talus, avoiding the cliff bands directly above.
waypoints.directions: Do not push straight up into the cliffs from the base of the talus: parties who take the direct line up the northeast side get cliffed out. Start a rising traverse to climber's left instead, holding the arc across loose talus and scree below the rock rather than gaining height too fast.

waypoints.name: North Side Scramble Start (~5000')
waypoints.note: On reaching the north side at about 5000', the final pitch splits: an easier Class 2 line on the right or a steeper Class 2/3 line straight up the center.
waypoints.directions: Hold the counterclockwise arc around onto the peak's north side, gaining a couple of hundred feet across talus to the broad bench. Fix the line in your head as you go — this traverse is what you reverse, and in poor visibility it is easy to drift back toward the cliff bands on the way down.

waypoints.name: Eagle Rock Summit
waypoints.note: True summit after roughly 600' of Class 2/3 scrambling from the north-side base; round trip from the car is typically under 3 hours.
waypoints.directions: From the bench, angle southwest a few hundred yards to the foot of the summit slope, then take about 600 vertical feet of open slope and talus to the top. A far-left finish adds around 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3; some parties carry a short length of rope to rig a handline there, though neither of the standard lines needs one.

before.pro_needs: None; the standard line is unroped scrambling terrain throughout.
before.best_season: Mid-July through October for the driest, most secure scrambling; because the standard line ascends the north-facing summit gully, snow/ice can linger there into early-to-mid July even after the approach slopes have cleared — carry an ice axe and check recent trip reports before a June/early-July attempt.
before.approach: Drive the Beckler River Road (FR-65) out of Skykomish and follow it into the FR-6510/FR-6514/FR-6517 spur network (about 10.8 miles of gravel/dirt forest road past the pavement) to road's end, roughly 0.5 mile east of Eagle Rock's summit at about 4,150 ft — this is the trailhead; there is no maintained trail beyond it. From the parking area, leave the road and head west/southwest straight up the hillside cross-country. You break out of brush and into open forest within the first few hundred feet, then continue uphill through timber; after a few hundred yards the trees give way to open talus slopes below the cliff bands on Eagle Rock's northeast side. From the base of the talus, do not push straight up into the cliffs — instead make an ascending, counterclockwise (climber's-left) traverse across and around the north side of the peak to a broad bench/step at roughly 5,000 ft. From that step, angle southwest a few hundred yards to the base of the final summit slope, where the scramble proper begins. One-way distance from the car to the summit is only about 0.8 mile, but essentially all of the route's ~1,400 ft of gain is packed into that short distance, so it feels considerably steeper than the mileage implies. There is no reliable water source anywhere on the approach — carry all the water you need from the car. Hazards are mostly footing and route-finding: loose talus and scree on the traverse, brush low down, no trail or cairns to follow, and cliff bands that will cliff out parties who try to go straight up the northeast talus instead of arcing counterclockwise. In late September 2024 the gate low on the Beckler spur network was locked, adding about ten miles of road each way; the road beyond it is rutted but passable to an AWD or high-clearance vehicle. Another party in early October found that gate closed but unlocked. Check before driving.
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, downclimb the same Class 2 (right side) or Class 2/3 (center) slope back down about 600 vertical feet to the ~5,000 ft bench, then reverse the counterclockwise talus traverse below the cliff bands back to treeline, and continue down through open forest and brush to the FR-6517 parking area. No technical anchors or rappels are needed on the standard line. The main descent hazards are loose talus/scree (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below) and route-finding — in poor visibility it's easy to drift toward the cliff bands instead of holding the correct counterclockwise line, so retrace your ascent traverse carefully. Parties who climbed the more exposed far-left finish (about 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3) sometimes downclimb that section more cautiously or carry ~50 ft of rope to rig an optional handline for extra security, but this is a personal-comfort choice on a minor variation, not a fixed rappel station, and the standard Class 2/3 line requires no rope at all. Parties in September and July used a short rappel (about 15-30 m) from a tree above the cliff band, or the fixed rope found at the steep forest bypass, to get down the crux section safely.
